cards.q: What does the Python interpreter do with a .py file?
cards.a: It turns the source into bytecode and runs it immediately, with no separate build step.
cards.lessonTitle: What Python Is and Running Code

cards.q: What is the difference between the interactive prompt and a script?
cards.a: The prompt runs one line at a time and shows each result; a script runs a whole file and shows only what it prints.
cards.lessonTitle: What Python Is and Running Code

cards.q: In Python, does the variable or the value have the type?
cards.a: The value; a variable is just a name and can refer to values of any type.

cards.q: What does int(3.99) give, and how do you round instead?
cards.a: 3, because int() cuts off the fraction; round(3.99) gives 4.

cards.q: What type does input() return?
cards.a: Always str, even when the user types a number.

cards.q: How do you print a float with two decimal places in an f-string?
cards.a: f"{value:.2f}"

cards.q: What are 7 / 2, 7 // 2 and 7 % 2?
Why should you not compare floats with ==?
cards.a: Most decimal fractions are stored approximately, so results that should be equal can differ in the last bits.

cards.q: What decides which lines belong to an if?
cards.a: Their indentation below the line with the colon.

cards.q: Why is `if x == 1 or 2:` always true?
cards.a: It means (x == 1) or 2, and 2 on its own is truthy.

cards.q: What does "Python"[1:4] give?
cards.a: "yth": from index 1 up to but not including 4.

cards.q: Why does word[0] = "J" fail?
cards.a: Strings are immutable; you build a new string instead.

cards.q: What is the difference between xs.sort() and sorted(xs)?
cards.a: sort() changes the list in place and returns None; sorted() returns a new sorted list.

cards.q: After b = a, does b.append(4) change a?
cards.a: Yes: both names refer to the same list. Copy with a.copy() to get a separate list.

cards.q: What numbers does range(10, 0, -3) produce?
When does a loop's else block run?
cards.a: When the loop ends without a break.

cards.q: How do you write a tuple with a single item?
cards.a: With a trailing comma: (42,).

cards.q: What does first, *rest = [1, 2, 3] give?
cards.a: first = 1 and rest = [2, 3].

cards.q: How do you read a key that may be missing without an error?
cards.a: d.get(key, default).

cards.q: What is {} on its own?
cards.a: An empty dictionary; an empty set is written set().

cards.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
cards.a: None.

cards.q: Why prefer returning a value over printing it inside the function?
cards.a: A returned value can be used in further calculations, tests and other functions; printed text cannot.

cards.q: Why is a list as a default value a bug?
cards.a: The default is created once and shared by every call, so changes from one call appear in the next.

cards.q: What does a bare * in a parameter list do?
cards.a: Makes every parameter after it keyword-only.

cards.q: In what order does Python look names up?
cards.a: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.

cards.q: What is a closure?
cards.a: A function together with variables from an enclosing function that it still refers to after that function has returned.

cards.q: What does if __name__ == "__main__": do?
cards.a: Runs the code below it only when the file is run directly, not when it is imported.

cards.q: Why should you not name your own file random.py?
cards.a: It shadows the standard library's random module, so import random imports your file.

cards.q: Why open files with a with block?
cards.a: The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even if an error occurs.

cards.q: What happens when you open an existing file with mode "w"?
cards.a: It is emptied before writing.

cards.q: What is self in a method?
cards.a: The instance the method was called on.

cards.q: What does a leading underscore on an attribute mean?
cards.a: It is internal to the class; other code should not use it directly.

cards.q: When are __str__ and __repr__ used?
cards.a: __str__ for print and f-strings; __repr__ for debugging output, and as a fallback for __str__.

cards.q: Why does 2 * v need __rmul__ when v * 2 only needs __mul__?
cards.a: With the number on the left, Python first asks int, which does not know vectors, and then calls the right operand's __rmul__.

cards.q: What does super().__init__(...) do in a subclass's __init__?
cards.a: Runs the base class's initialisation so its part of the object is set up.

cards.q: What is duck typing?
cards.a: Code works with any object that has the methods it uses, regardless of the object's class.

cards.q: What does @dataclass write for you?
cards.a: __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ (and more with options), from the annotated fields.

cards.q: Why must a list default be written field(default_factory=list)?
cards.a: A plain list default would be shared by every instance.

cards.q: Which line of a traceback do you read first?
cards.a: The last one: the exception type and message.

cards.q: Why catch specific exceptions instead of everything?
cards.a: Catching everything also hides real bugs such as typos and wrong types.

cards.q: What is the difference between [x for x in xs if c] and [a if c else b for x in xs]?
cards.a: The first filters items out; the second keeps every item but chooses a value for each.

cards.q: Why is sum(x * x for x in data) better than sum([x * x for x in data]) for big data?
cards.a: The generator expression produces values one at a time instead of building a whole list in memory.

cards.q: What happens when a generator function is called?
cards.a: It returns a generator without running the body; the body runs step by step as values are requested.

cards.q: Why can a generator process a file bigger than memory?
cards.a: It yields one item at a time, so only the current item needs to be in memory.

cards.q: How do you sort by score descending and then by name ascending?
cards.a: key=lambda r: (-r.score, r.name)

cards.q: What does stable sorting guarantee?
cards.a: Items with equal keys keep the order they had before sorting.

cards.q: What does a Counter return for a key it has never seen?
cards.a: 0, instead of raising KeyError.

cards.q: Why must items be sorted before itertools.groupby?
cards.a: It groups only consecutive items with the same key.

cards.q: Does Python check type hints when the program runs?
cards.a: No; they are used by editors and type checkers such as mypy and Pyright.

cards.q: What does pytest.mark.parametrize do?
cards.a: Runs the same test function once for each set of arguments.

cards.q: Why write patterns as raw strings?
cards.a: So backslashes such as \d reach the re module instead of being treated as Python escapes.

cards.q: Which function checks that a whole string has a given form?
cards.a: re.fullmatch.

cards.q: Why should CSV not be split with line.split(",")?
cards.a: Quoted fields can contain commas (and quotes and new lines); the csv module handles them.

cards.q: What type does every CSV field have when read?
cards.a: str: numbers must be converted explicitly.

cards.q: Why is ISO 8601 the best format for storing dates?
cards.a: It is unambiguous, sorts correctly as text, and is parsed directly by fromisoformat.

cards.q: What is a naive datetime?
cards.a: One without time zone information.

cards.q: What does exit code 0 mean?
cards.a: Success; any other value means the program failed.

cards.q: Why should a script that renames files have a dry-run mode?
cards.a: To show exactly what would change before anything is changed.

cards.q: Why does read_rows take lines rather than a file path?
cards.a: So tests can pass a list of strings without creating files; main does the file handling.

cards.q: Why compute revenue in whole cents?
cards.a: Integer arithmetic is exact, so totals over many rows have no floating-point error.

cards.q: What does `@log_calls` above a `def` do?
cards.a: It replaces the function with `log_calls(function)`: whatever the decorator returns is what the name refers to from then on.

cards.q: Why does a decorator with arguments need three nested functions?
cards.a: The outer one takes the arguments and returns the real decorator; the decorator takes the function and returns the wrapper; the wrapper runs on each call.

cards.q: When does `__exit__` run?
cards.a: Whenever the body ends: normally, by `return` or `break`, or with an exception.

cards.q: In a `@contextmanager` function, why put the cleanup in `finally`?
cards.a: If the body raises, the exception is thrown into the generator at the `yield`; without `finally` the code after it would be skipped.

cards.q: Why use a descriptor instead of properties?
cards.a: One descriptor class holds a rule (such as "must be positive") that many attributes in many classes can share; properties would repeat it each time.

cards.q: What does `ABC` with `@abstractmethod` prevent?
cards.a: Creating an object of a class that still has methods left to fill in.

cards.q: Why does `case RED:` not compare with a constant named `RED`?
cards.a: A bare name in a pattern always captures (and so always matches). Use a dotted name like `Color.RED` to compare with a constant.

cards.q: Does `{"type": "key"}` match a dictionary with extra keys?
cards.a: Yes. Mapping patterns check only the keys they name; `**rest` collects the others.

cards.q: Why do threads speed up downloading but not adding up numbers in pure Python?
cards.a: A waiting thread releases the GIL so others can run; a calculating thread holds it, so only one calculates at a time.

cards.q: What does a `Lock` protect against?
cards.a: Two threads changing shared data at the same time and losing one of the changes (a race condition).

cards.q: What happens when you call an `async def` function without awaiting it?
cards.a: Nothing runs: you get a coroutine object, and Python warns that it was never awaited.

cards.q: Why is `time.sleep(1)` inside a coroutine a bug?
cards.a: It blocks the only thread, so the event loop cannot run any other task for that second.

cards.q: Why write `log.info("x is %s", x)` instead of `log.info(f"x is {x}")`?
cards.a: The values are only turned into text if the message is shown, so switched-off messages cost almost nothing; tools can also group messages by their unformatted text.

cards.q: Where should `basicConfig` be called?
cards.a: Once, at the program's start, in the entry point. Modules only call `getLogger(__name__)` and log.

cards.q: Why does `setUp` run before every test, not once?
cards.a: So each test starts from the same fresh state and cannot be affected by what another test changed.

cards.q: Code calls `datetime.now()` directly. How can a test control the time?
cards.a: Patch the name where the code looks it up, or (better) change the code to take a clock or a time as a parameter.

cards.q: What does Python do when a value does not match its hint?
cards.a: Nothing at run time. Hints are read by type checkers and editors, which report the problem before the program runs.

cards.q: Why `def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T` rather than `-> object`?
cards.a: With the type parameter, the checker knows `first(["a"])` is a `str` and lets you call string methods on it.

cards.q: What does `len("é".encode("utf-8"))` give, and why?
cards.a: 2: UTF-8 stores `é` (code point 233) in two bytes.

cards.q: Why does a struct format string start with `<` or `>`?
cards.a: To fix the byte order, so the bytes mean the same on every machine instead of following the computer the code happens to run on.

cards.q: Why `?` placeholders instead of an f-string?
cards.a: They keep values as data, so text from a user can never change the SQL command (SQL injection), and quoting is handled for you.

cards.q: What happens to changes made inside `with con:` when the block raises?
cards.a: They are rolled back; nothing from that block is saved.

cards.q: Why give every project its own virtual environment?
cards.a: So each project gets exactly the package versions it needs, without affecting other projects or the system's Python.

cards.q: What does `[project.scripts]` in `pyproject.toml` do?
cards.a: It creates a command that runs a chosen function when the package is installed.
